extracted.intended_audience: agency rulemakers, administrative law scholars, and policymakers interested in e-rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Survey-based evaluation of how the advent of electronic rulemaking (e-rulemaking/FDMS/regulations.gov) has affected agency processes, public participation, comment quality, security/privacy concerns, and administrative efficiency/quality of rules. The page lists specific operational tasks and worries and reports respondent summaries/statistics for each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct proactive notification and outreach by maintaining target mailing lists (or listservs)
rubrics_metrics.description: When compared to the old system of paper comments, has the advent of e-rulemaking made it more difficult or easier for your agency to conduct proactive notification and outreach to the public by maintaining target mailing lists (or listservs) of people interested in aspects of your rulemaking agendas?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1 (much more difficult) to 7 (much easier). Response Count: 64; Average Score: 5.51 (n=37). Used to measure whether e-rulemaking facilitates targeted outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and find appropriate stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking made it easier or harder to identify and find appropriate stakeholders?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 64; Average Score: 4.81 (n=42). Measures discoverability of stakeholders via electronic tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disseminate information relevant to proposed rulemaking to generate more informed commenters
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking affected the agency's ability to disseminate studies, economic analyses, legal analyses, etc., so as to generate more informed commenters?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 64; Average Score: 5.67 (n=46). Captures effectiveness of online dockets in sharing supporting materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present competing or multiple alternatives to the proposed rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking changed the agency's ability to present competing or multiple alternatives to the proposed rules to the public?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 63; Average Score: 4.73 (n=37). Relates to presenting options and public visibility of alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stimulate public comments generally
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking made it easier or harder to stimulate public comments generally?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 64; Average Score: 5.33 (n=51). Used as a measure of e-rulemaking's effect on overall participation levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sort and analyze public comments generally
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking affected the agency's ability to sort and analyze public comments in general?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 64; Average Score: 5.02 (n=51). Captures perceived analytic/management benefits or burdens of electronic comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain public comments specifically addressed to particular portions or segments of the proposed rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking changed the agency's ability to obtain comments that are addressed to particular sections or portions of the proposed rule?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 64; Average Score: 4.64 (n=47). Measures targeted commentary elicitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sort and analyze public comments specifically addressed to particular portions
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking affected the ability to sort and analyze comments that address particular portions or segments of the proposed rule?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 64; Average Score: 4.70 (n=46). Focuses on topic-specific organization and review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the concept of 'reply comments'
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking affected your agency's use of reply comments (comments responding to other comments)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 59; Average Score: 5.44 (n=25). Measures facilitation of iterative commenter interaction (reply comments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Place summaries of ex parte communications in the record more quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking made it easier or harder to place summaries of ex parte communications in the record more quickly?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 58; Average Score: 5.16 (n=38). Relates to timeliness of documenting ex parte contacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate the rulemaking internally by allowing many people to look at the same docket without getting in each other's way
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking helped or hindered internal coordination by allowing multiple staff to view the same docket concurrently without interference?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 59; Average Score: 5.70 (n=43). Measures collaboration benefits of shared electronic access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate the rulemaking externally with OMB or other interested government entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking affected the agency's ability to coordinate rulemaking externally with OMB or other interested government entities?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 62; Average Score: 5.23 (n=40). Captures cross-government coordination effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct interactive proceedings in rulemaking (e.g., negotiated rulemaking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking affected the agency's ability to conduct interactive proceedings such as negotiated rulemaking?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 59; Average Score: 4.19 (n=16). Assesses e-rulemaking's role in facilitating interactive formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft a preamble to the final rule that responds to comments and includes all relevant studies and analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking made it easier or harder to craft a preamble that adequately responds to comments and incorporates relevant studies/analyses?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 60; Average Score: 5.05 (n=44). Relates to completeness and responsiveness in final-rule documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and implement appropriate archival practices relating to rulemakings (such as retiring records)
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking affected the agency's ability to develop and implement archival practices for rulemakings (e.g., retiring records)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 58; Average Score: 5.25 (n=36). Measures archival/records-management implications of electronic dockets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodically evaluate and review the rule (and related rules) once promulgated
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking changed the agency's ability to periodically evaluate and review promulgated rules and related rules?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 62; Average Score: 5.19 (n=37). Captures post-promulgation oversight and review capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outside intervention ('hacking') into rulemaking proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: When compared to the old paper system, has the advent of e-rulemaking caused your agency to worry more or less about outside intervention ("hacking") into your rulemaking proceedings?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1 (worry much more) to 7 (worry much less). Response Count: 62; Average Score: 3.32 (n=37). Used to measure cybersecurity concern increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquiring viruses via attachments submitted in comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking changed the agency's level of worry about acquiring viruses via attachments submitted in comments?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 62; Average Score: 3.31 (n=36). Measures IT-safety concerns tied to public submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inappropriate exposure of materials that might contain confidential business information
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking caused more or less worry about inappropriate exposure of docket materials that might contain confidential business information?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 62; Average Score: 3.11 (n=45). Noted as one of the higher worries (lowest average scores). Attorney respondents even more worried.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inappropriate exposure of materials that might contain copyrighted materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking changed worry about inappropriate exposure of docket materials that might contain copyrighted materials?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 62; Average Score: 3.20 (n=46). Identified as a significant concern among respondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inappropriate exposure of materials that might contain indecent or obscene language or materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking affected worry about inappropriate exposure of docket materials that might contain indecent or obscene language or materials?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 62; Average Score: 3.30 (n=44). Raised as a notable concern; attorneys more worried on some categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inappropriate exposure of information that might lead to national security problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking increased worry about exposure of information in dockets that might lead to national security problems?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 62; Average Score: 3.82 (n=28). Measures national-security-related disclosure concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of information-destruction or other irretrievable loss of rulemaking information
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking changed the agency's worry about information-destruction or irretrievable loss of rulemaking information?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 62; Average Score: 4.09 (n=43). One of two hypothesized concerns that were less worrisome under e-rulemaking (average >4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrating (scanned) paper comments with e-mailed or electronically submitted comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking affected the agency's worry or ability regarding integrating scanned paper comments with e-mailed or electronically submitted comments?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response scale 1–7. Response Count: 62; Average Score: 4.14 (n=49). Also listed earlier as becoming less worrisome under e-rulemaking (average 4.14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of comments (volume of public comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Has the advent of e-rulemaking led to more or fewer public comments (volume)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorical responses reported (Many Fewer ... Many More). Response Count: 50; Average Score: 5.36 (n=45). Thirty-one of forty-seven respondents who experienced both systems reported some increase; used to measure participation volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comments that provide new useful information or arguments (usefulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking led to more or fewer comments that provide new useful information or arguments?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses split; Average Score: 3.80 (n=44); three-fifths indicated no difference. Measures substantive quality of increased commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comments that provide only opinions without supporting facts or arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking produced more or fewer comments that provide only opinions without supporting facts or arguments?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No respondents reported fewer; many reported increases. Response Count: 50; Average Score: 2.81 (n=42). Indicates perceived decline in evidentiary quality among some comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comments that are identical or nearly identical (duplication/mass campaigns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking produced more or fewer comments that are identical or nearly identical?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High number of respondents reported increases; many answered 'many more.' Response Count: 49; Average Score: 2.59 (n=39). Captures concern about mass/identical submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived value of comments by the average citizen
rubrics_metrics.description: Has e-rulemaking affected how much value agencies place on the comments of the average citizen?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most reported 'the same.' Response Count: 50; Average Score: 4.27 (n=50). Measures whether increased volume changes evaluative weight given to average citizen input.

rubrics_metrics.name: More commenters responding to others' comments (interaction among commenters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Have you seen more commenters responding to comments already in the docket with the advent of e-rulemaking?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yes/No/Don't Know responses reported; 20 yes, 16 no, 14 don't know (n=50). Measures increased inter-commenter dialogue or reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: More references to economic analyses and other supporting documents in the docket
rubrics_metrics.description: With e-rulemaking, have commenters made more references to economic analyses and other supporting documents in the docket?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses: 7 yes, 22 no, 20 don't know. Suggests limited change in citation of supporting documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of public questions to the office about ongoing rulemakings
rubrics_metrics.description: Has the number of questions agencies receive about ongoing rulemakings changed with e-rulemaking?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response Count: 50; Average Score: 4.21 (n=39). Indicates a slight increase in questions received (many reported 'the same' or slight increases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity to consult with and learn from counterparts in other agencies about e-rulemaking issues
rubrics_metrics.description: How much opportunity have agency rulemakers had to consult with and learn from counterparts in other agencies about e-rulemaking issues?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More than half reported that opportunity was less than adequate; categorical responses reported (None, Minimal, Adequate, Great). Captures inter-agency knowledge-sharing adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether agency makes hard (paper) copies of e-comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Do agency rulemakers make hard (paper) copies of electronic comments (and how often)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Of 59 responses: 8 'never', 24 'occasionally', 9 'usually', 18 'always'. Narrative reasons: legal requirements, litigation needs, difficulty reviewing long electronic comments, sharing with colleagues without e-access. Measures hybrid paper-electronic workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of computer-based 'sorting' technology to categorize or identify duplicate e-comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the agency use computer-based sorting technology to help categorize or identify duplicate e-comments, and how helpful is it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Of 59 respondents, 20 didn't know; of those knowing, 17 yes, 22 no. Helpfulness among 12: 3 very helpful, 6 helpful, 2 a little helpful, 1 not at all. Two agencies hired contractors. Measures automation adoption and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: E-rulemaking's effect on agency efficiency in promulgating rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall, has the advent of e-rulemaking allowed your agency to promulgate rules less or more efficiently?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response Count: 50; Average Score: 4.61 (n=44). Twenty-three of forty-four reported an increase in efficiency vs. eight reporting a decline. Used as a bottom-line efficiency metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: E-rulemaking's effect on promulgating higher quality rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall, has e-rulemaking made it less or more easy for your agency to promulgate higher quality rules?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response Count: 50; Average Score: 4.36 (n=44). Twelve of forty-four reported an increase in quality and five reported a decrease; more respondents answered 'the same' than for efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of e-dockets for actions other than rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the agency use electronic dockets for actions other than rulemaking (adjudication, guidances, notices, correspondence, etc.)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Of 59 respondents, 36 reported use of e-dockets for other actions, 23 did not. Narrative examples (adjudications, policy statements, filing systems) illustrate broader e-docket adoption and perceived transparency benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative perceptions: 'boon for the public but a bane for the agency'
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative judgments about e-rulemaking's overall impact—e.g., better public access but new administrative burdens for agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative responses summarize common themes: improved public access, internal coordination gains, but technical glitches, maintenance of dual systems, difficulties in sorting/printing, concerns about authenticity, and training/learning-curve burdens. Use as interpretive context rather than a single numeric metric.
